credulous

KREJ-uh-lus · adjective

Hear It

What It Means

Credulous is too trusting or easily fooled; ready to believe things without enough evidence.

The credulous new employee believed every wild rumor the office prankster told him during his first week.

Example

The credulous audience applauded the magician's 'real magic' claim without ever suspecting a hidden trick.

Credulous describes a readiness to believe claims without enough evidence or healthy skepticism.

Your Turn

Compare the words

Synonyms · words with a similar meaning

gullible: Gullible means easily tricked: a gullible person falls for pranks and scams because they miss the deception aimed at them. Credulous is broader and a shade more formal — a credulous person stands ready to believe any claim without asking for evidence, even when nobody is deliberately trying to fool them.

unsuspecting: Unsuspecting describes a moment, not a character: someone unaware, right then, that a trick or danger is coming. Credulous is a lasting habit of mind — a credulous person keeps accepting claims without enough evidence, situation after situation. You can be unsuspecting once; credulous describes what you are like every day.

What it isn’t · antonyms and near-opposites

skeptical: having doubts about claims until they are proven

wary: cautious about possible danger or problems

Where it sits · how easily belief is handed over

trusting → credulous → unquestioning

trusting vs. credulous: Trusting is a general, positive quality; credulous adds a critical edge, implying that trust is given too easily, without good reason.

unquestioning vs. credulous: Unquestioning goes further than credulous, implying someone accepts claims with absolutely no doubt or scrutiny at all.

Build the Word

The pieces

root — cred: to believe (Latin (credere))

suffix — -ulous: full of, inclined to (Latin)

Put it together: cred- ('to believe') + -ulous ('full of, inclined to') together mean 'inclined to believe' -- exactly the too-trusting quality credulous describes.

Use the root in a new word: credit: The word credit grew from the same Latin root credere and traveled through banking into everyday English.
